title: Ἀλώπηξ κολουρός
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 41. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἀλώπηξ ὑπό τινος πάγης τὴν οὐρὰν ἀποκοπεῖσα, ἐπειδὴ δι’ αἰσχύνην ἀβίωτον ἡγεῖτο τὸν βίον ἔχειν, ἔγνω δεῖν καὶ τὰς ἄλλας ἀλώπεκας εἰς τὸ αὐτὸ προαγαγεῖν, ἵνα τῷ κοινῷ πάθει τὸ ἴδιον ἐλάττωμα συγκρύψῃ.
sentences.tr: Alōpēx hypo tinos pagēs tēn ouran apokopeisa, epeidē di’ aischynēn abiōton hēgeito ton bion echein, egnō dein kai tas allas alōpekas eis to auto proagagein, hina tōi koinōi pathei to idion elattōma synkrypsēi.
sentences.l: A fox, having had her tail cut off by a certain trap, since for shame she considered that she had a life not worth living, resolved that she must bring the other foxes too into the same state, so that by the common suffering she might hide her own defect.
sentences.i: A fox lost her tail in a trap; and since for shame she thought life not worth living, she resolved to bring the other foxes to the same pass, so that a shared trouble might cover her own defect.
sentences.n: τὴν οὐράν is an accusative of respect with the passive participle ἀποκοπεῖσα: “cut off as to her tail.” Greek can name the person and the part affected in one stroke where English needs a possessive. ἵνα with the aorist subjunctive (συγκρύψῃ) gives the purpose; the συν- of συγκρύψῃ answers the κοινῷ of κοινῷ πάθει — a shared trouble is a covering.

sentences.t: Καὶ δὴ ἁπάσας ἀθροίσασα παρῄνει αὐταῖς τὰς οὐρὰς ἀποκόπτειν, λέγουσα ὡς οὐκ ἀπρεπὲς μόνον τοῦτο, ἀλλὰ καὶ περισσόν τι αὐταῖς βάρος προσήρτηται.
sentences.tr: Kai dē hapasas athroisasa parēinei autais tas ouras apokoptein, legousa hōs ouk aprepes monon touto, alla kai perisson ti autais baros prosērtētai.
sentences.l: And so, having gathered them all, she urged them to cut off their tails, saying that this was not merely unseemly, but that a superfluous weight of some kind had been hung upon them as well.
sentences.n: οὐ μόνον … ἀλλὰ καί, “not only … but also,” is the standard pair. προσήρτηται is a perfect passive of προσαρτᾶν, “to fasten on” — the tail is treated as an appendage already attached, not as part of the animal. ὡς after λέγουσα introduces reported speech.

sentences.t: Τούτων δέ τις ὑποτυχοῦσα ἔφη· « Ὦ αὕτη, ἀλλ’ εἰ ⟨μή⟩ σοι τοῦτο συνέφερεν, οὐκ ἂν ἡμῖν τοῦτο συνεβούλευσας. »
sentences.tr: Toutōn de tis hypotychousa ephē· « Ō hautē, all’ ei ⟨mē⟩ soi touto synepheren, ouk an hēmin touto synebouleusas. »
sentences.l: And one of them, taking her up, said: « You there — but if this were ⟨not⟩ to your own advantage, you would not have advised it to us. »
sentences.i: One of them broke in and said, “You there! If this were not to your own advantage, you would never have recommended it to us.”
sentences.n: Chambry prints ⟨μή⟩ in angle brackets: the word is not in the manuscripts, and he supplies it, since without it the sentence says the opposite of what it must mean. Throughout this edition ⟨ ⟩ marks what the editor adds and [ ] what he judges intrusive and strikes out — the text is a reconstruction, and it shows its seams. The condition is contrary to fact: imperfect in the “if” clause, aorist with ἄν in the conclusion. Ὦ αὕτη is a blunt way of hailing a female — “hey, you.”

sentences.t: Οὗτος ὁ λόγος ἁρμόττει πρὸς ἐκείνους οἳ τὰς συμβουλίας ποιοῦνται τοῖς πέλας οὐ δι’ εὔνοιαν, ἀλλὰ διὰ τὸ ἑαυτοῖς συμφέρον.
sentences.tr: Houtos ho logos harmottei pros ekeinous hoi tas symboulias poiountai tois pelas ou di’ eunoian, alla dia to heautois sympheron.
sentences.l: This story fits those who offer their counsel to their neighbours not out of goodwill, but for the sake of their own advantage.
sentences.n: A closing formula of its own shape: οὗτος ὁ λόγος ἁρμόττει πρός…, “this story fits…”, naming the people it is aimed at rather than stating a rule. οἱ πέλας, “those close by,” is ordinary Greek for one's neighbours. τὸ ἑαυτοῖς συμφέρον is a participle used as a noun: “the thing advantageous to themselves.”
